claims.text: Controlled nanoscale secondary-phase precipitation in an fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti HEA can raise coercivity above 100 Oe.
Ti-rich or Fe-Ti intermetallic precipitates such as Fe2Ti, or L10-ordered precipitates, can be ferromagnetic or hard-magnetic while remaining embedded in an fcc matrix.
The secondary phase will pin magnetic domain walls and overcome the effect of orbital-moment suppression in the fcc matrix.
At suitable Ti concentrations and annealing temperatures, thermodynamic instability of the fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti matrix will drive coherent or semi-coherent precipitation.
Coherent or semi-coherent precipitate interfaces will generate local strain fields and magnetic-anisotropy barriers.
Strain fields and exchange coupling at precipitate-matrix interfaces will enhance effective anisotropy energy and thereby increase coercivity.
Negative mixing enthalpy of Fe-Ti or Co-Ti pairs can stabilize the proposed Ti-containing secondary phase.
A solutionized, single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti alloy has low coercivity because of suppressed orbital moments and a lack of pinning sites.
Aging at 400–600 °C after solution annealing can promote secondary-phase nucleation while retaining the fcc matrix.
A Ti concentration of 5–15 at.% provides sufficient precipitation driving force while maintaining fcc-matrix stability.
Matching precipitate size and distribution to the magnetic domain-wall width maximizes pinning force.
The proposed alloy will retain the required magnetic behavior at operating temperatures above 300 K, including at 400 K.
After aging, the alloy will exhibit coercivity above 100 Oe.
After aging, saturation magnetization will decrease by 20–40% relative to the single-phase state.
The reduction in saturation magnetization will result from non-magnetic or lower-moment precipitates and the pinning effect.
The aged alloy will have a hysteresis-loop squareness ratio greater than 0.5.
A single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti baseline has coercivity below 10 Oe and high saturation magnetization.
Ti contents above 15 at.% may destabilize the fcc matrix and cause excessive phase separation or amorphization that degrades magnetic properties.
Aging above 700 °C may coarsen precipitates, reduce pinning efficiency, and lower coercivity below 100 Oe.
Phase-separated AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi has exhibited a coercivity of 39.4 Oe.

contradictions.description: The precipitate is proposed as a ferromagnetic or hard-magnetic phase, but the predicted magnetization loss is attributed to the precipitates being non-magnetic or lower-moment. These alternatives are not resolved into a consistent phase-selection constraint.

The hypothesis says secondary precipitation is required for coercivity above 100 Oe, whereas the first falsification condition treats absence of precipitates together with low coercivity as falsifying that requirement. That result is actually consistent with, rather than contrary to, the proposed necessity of precipitates.
